analysis: The two units are head-side excerpts of fixtures/prompt-contract/v1/production_vectors.json, lines 17217-18743. They contain gemma-4-26b-8bit prompt-contract vectors: chat_completions, messages, responses, tool turns, an exact 256-token block multiple, and a 600-token plan with 256/512 block boundaries. The patch excerpt for this file also shows changes elsewhere, including additional_context enable_thinking=false, a changed token count, changed chain hashes and removed token IDs. Those changed ranges were not in the supplied units, so they were not reviewed. The viewed regions are static test data. They hold synthetic prompts such as 'Completion endpoint', 'Be concise.' and 'Check the current weather and forecast.', fixed dates, public token IDs and hex chain hashes. I found no secrets, credentials, keys, attestation material or production data. I also found no executable code, authorization logic, new endpoints, or changes to WebSocket, attestation, encryption or App Attest handling (TB-002, TB-009, TB-011). The only plausible threat surface is T-041, the prefix-cache and block-hash contract. The visible chain hashes are consistent with deterministic fixture values, and the excerpts show no cross-tenant scope weakening: every case uses scope_id 'fixture-scope', and chain hashes are computed by code that is not supplied here. Integration questions: whether the Swift and Go prompt-plan implementations that consume these fixtures enforce the same scoping and block-hash derivation (T-041), and whether the unviewed changed ranges, such as the removal of the 768-token block and the additional_context change, still match the code that consumes them. Fixtures cannot change runtime security behavior by themselves. No security regression was identified in the reviewed lines.
